title: Hearing With Your Eyes
objective: After this level you can explain the McGurk effect and how the mind merges what you see with what you hear.
summary: In the McGurk effect, the sound "ba" with a face saying "ga" is often heard as "da": the brain merges sight and sound. How strongly people are fooled varies widely.

cards.headline: Your eyes can change what you hear.
cards.body: Play a recording of someone saying one syllable, but show a face mouthing a different one. Many people hear a third syllable that neither the voice nor the lips produced. Heard alone, without the video, the same sound is identified almost perfectly.

cards.headline: Hearing lips and seeing voices
cards.body: That's the McGurk effect, reported by Harry McGurk and John MacDonald in 1976 in a paper titled "Hearing lips and seeing voices". In their report, 98 percent of adults heard "da" when the sound "ba" was paired with a video of lips saying "ga". The mismatch doesn't make you hear the voice or read the lips: you hear a third syllable, different from both.

cards.headline: Why the brain blends
cards.body: Your brain integrates information from different senses, and it typically responds more strongly to sight and sound together than to the sum of each alone. That's useful: at a loud concert, watching a friend's lips helps you follow what they say, while in a quiet cafe you'd hardly need it. The McGurk effect is reported to be strongest when the sound is poor, when your eyes have the most to add.

cards.fact: In a 2015 study of 165 adults, some never heard the illusion and some heard it every time.
cards.context: How often people heard it ranged from 0 to 100 percent, and it also varied with the video used. The effect is real, but that famous 98 percent came from one stimulus, and how strongly you're fooled depends a lot on who you are and what you watch.

mascot.line: Don't memorize the 98 percent. Remember the lesson: one famous number rarely tells the whole story.

cards.headline: Hearing with your eyes
learned: McGurk effect (1976): "ba" plus lips "ga" sounds like "da"
The brain merges sight and sound
Lips help most when sound is poor

questions.prompt: In the classic McGurk effect, the sound "ba" paired with lips saying "ga" makes many people hear _____.

options.label: "ba"
options.rationale: That's the sound alone, heard without the video.

options.label: "ga"
options.rationale: That's what the lips say, not what's heard.

options.label: silence
options.rationale: People hear a syllable, just not the one played.

questions.explanation: In McGurk and MacDonald's 1976 report, 98 percent of adults heard "da": a third syllable that fuses the two.

questions.prompt: Why does watching a friend's lips help you understand them at a loud concert?

options.label: The brain merges sight and sound
Loud music switches off your hearing
options.rationale: You still hear; sight adds to it.

options.label: Lip-reading replaces sound completely
options.rationale: The two are integrated, not swapped.

options.label: Everyone at concerts has trained in lip-reading
options.rationale: No training is involved; the brain does it.

questions.explanation: Information from different senses is integrated, and responses to sight and sound together are stronger, which helps most when the sound is poor.

questions.prompt: Match each McGurk effect finding with its number.
questions.explanation: Harry McGurk and John MacDonald reported the effect in 1976. A 2015 study of 165 adults found that how often people heard it ranged from 0 to 100 percent.
